description: human resource management policies and practices. The first cluster concentrates on the topics related to HRM policies and practices, and it is by far the largest cluster in PR, which suggests that much of the focus of PR authors have been on the bread-and-butter issues of HRM. The articles in this cluster have examined topics such as HR practices in small- and medium-sized firms, HR practices related to training, HR leadership within organizations, the effect of HR practices on employee attitudes, and the promotion of diversity and empowerment within the workforce. The journal in its early years seems to have focused exclusively on topics in this theme as Figure 4 shows that this cluster dominated the PR corpus in the first four decades of the journal’s run. However, newer topics have emerged, resulting in the genuine establishment of new themes, which will be revealed in the next sections. Nevertheless, this cluster remains the core of PR, as the topics under this theme are fundamental to our understanding of HRM. The most cited article in this cluster is Wilkinson’s (1998) article, which focuses on employee empowerment, followed by Cassell et al.’s (2002) article on HR practices in smalland medium-sized firms, and Axtell et al.’s (1997) article on the factors affecting training effectiveness. These articles are the top three cited articles in this cluster, which have garnered 239, 163, and 158 citations, respectively.

personnel competency, experience, and well-being The second cluster focuses on the behavioral aspects of HR in terms of personnel competency, experience, and well-being, and it is flagged as the most popular area of HRM research among PR authors in recent years. The articles in this cluster have explored topics such as time management, work-family conflict, training motivation, person-organization value congruence, behavior of leadership, psychological empowerment of employees, emotional intelligence, workaholism within organization, employee well-being, work intrinsic motivation, innovative behavior among employees, horizontal and vertical communication within organization, and abusive supervision. These topics seem to have arisen out of the topics from the first cluster, where the focus was on HRM policies and practices, which have a bearing on the behavior of employees. In that sense, HRM research in this cluster represents the perspective of employees rather than the organization. Noteworthily, Figure 4 suggests that this cluster is a relatively new yet popular cluster that has emerged notably between 2001 and 2010 and proliferated exponentially between 2011 and 2020. The most cited article in this cluster is Claessens et al.’s (2007) article, which delivers a literature review on time management, followed by the articles co-authored by Fu and Shaffer (2001) and Rotondo et al. (2003), which focused on the issue of work-family conflict. These articles, which represent the top three cited articles in this cluster, have been cited 209, 174, and 121 times, respectively.

career management and employee engagement The third cluster encapsulates HRM research on career management and employee engagement, and it is the most popular area of research between 2001 and 2010, and continues to remain as a (second most) popular area of research among PR authors between 2011 and 2020. The articles in this cluster have investigated topics such as self-perceived employability, work ethic, employer branding, self-directed expatriation, expatriate adjustment, passioncareer satisfaction, organizational identification, and perceived diversity at demographical and psychological levels. Though the topics in this cluster have largely focused on employees, some attention has been given to organizational practices as well. Noteworthily, Figure 4 indicates that this cluster has also developed much later in the journal’s run, gaining prominence in the 2000s, and since then, the theme of this cluster has garnered burgeoning attention from PR authors, as seen through its increasing share of publications in the journal’s corpus. The most cited article in this cluster is Rothwell and Arnold’s (2007) article, which develops a scale for self-perceived employability, followed by Yousef’s (2001) article on Islamic work ethic and its relationship between organizational commitment and job satisfaction, and Edwards’ (2009) literature review on employer branding. These articles are the top three cited articles in this cluster that have received 298, 200, and 161 citations, respectively.

strategic human resource management The fourth cluster is dedicated to strategic HRM, which involves a future-oriented outlook of managing human capital in the organization, and it is the third most popular area of research among PR authors in recent years. The articles in this cluster have explored topics such as knowledge transfer, the effect of HR strategy on employee behavior and turnover intention, employee development and growth in intellectual capital, institutional pressures, the relationship between business strategy and HR strategy, talent management of employees, outsourcing of HR, and highcommitment and high-performance workplaces. The theme of this cluster emerged notably between 2001 and 2010 and proliferated exponentially along with the second, third, and fifth clusters between 2011 and 2020, as seen in Figure 4. The most cited article in this cluster is Minbaeva’s (2005) article, which examines the practices of knowledge transfer within multinational corporations, followed by Kroon et al.’s (2009) article on the effect of high-performance work practices on employee burnout, and Prieto and P erez-Santana’s (2014) article on the effect of high-involvement HR practices on employee innovation. These three articles, which represent the top three cited articles in this cluster, have been cited 122, 100, and 94 times, respectively.

organizational culture and workplace environment The fifth and final cluster pertains to organizational culture and workplace environment, and like the three preceding clusters, this cluster began its development only in the 2000s and continues to proliferate in the 2010s. The articles in this cluster have investigated topics such as organizational trust, work team trust and effectiveness, organizational citizenship behaviors, organizational politics, organizational policies on sexual harassment and discrimination, relationships within different levels of the organization, organizational justice, and the impact of organizational culture and workplace environment on employee performance and productivity. The most cited article in this cluster is Dietz and Den Hartog’s (2006) article, which develops the measures of intra-organizational trust, followed by Costa’s (2003) article on the effect of work team trust on employee effectiveness, and Wat and Shaffer’s (2005) article on the mediating role of trust on organizational citizenship behavior and empowerment. These top three cited articles have received 262, 218, and 150 citations, respectively.
